v.rationale: All three put points and the shipment inside a transaction and send the mail with DB::afterCommit, so outer rollbacks leave no side effects and all pass their suites. impl-1 and impl-2 use the same atomic conditional-UPDATE claim. impl-1 ranks first because it keeps the domain exception HTTP-agnostic and renders the 409 centrally, uses fluent ->can() with a policy, guards user_id against mass assignment, and has the broadest tests (rounding datasets, validation messages, rollback on a failed shipment insert). Its probe flaws are minor: 500 for a non-JSON guest, and a policy TypeError on a user without is_staff loaded. impl-2 is nearly as good and is the only one that handles non-JSON guests correctly. It loses ground because its exception extends ConflictHttpException, putting HTTP inside the model that back-office code calls, and because of an odd manual DB::rollBack in its test; it shares the policy null-bool issue. impl-3 ranks third: its lockForUpdate approach is valid on real databases, but it catches the 409 in the controller, checks staff in FormRequest::authorize instead of a policy, leaves the caller's model dirty after ship(), returns 500 for non-JSON guests, and has thinner tests.
